client: I've been really struggling since last week when our team missed a major project deadline. I'm new to this project manager role and I feel like everything is falling apart — like I'm constantly drowning in tasks and I can't keep my head above water. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the pressure is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — stepping into a new leadership role and facing a missed deadline right away is genuinely a lot to carry, and I want you to know that feeling is valid. You're right that our conversation won't make the pressure disappear, but sometimes just understanding what's driving that "drowning" feeling can help you find one small foothold rather than treading water alone. I'm curious — when you imagine "everything falling apart," what's the specific fear that feels most loud for you right now?

client: I think the loudest fear is that people are going to realize I don't actually know what I'm doing — like, that I only got this role because someone made a mistake in hiring me. When the deadline was missed, it felt like proof of that, and I keep waiting for my manager to pull me aside and tell me it's over. It's like I'm constantly bracing for the moment everything gets confirmed.
therapist: What you're describing — this fear of being "found out" as not truly qualified — is something many people experience when they step into a new or challenging role, and it even has a name: impostor syndrome. I want to gently ask you to examine that thought that the missed deadline is *proof* you don't belong, because one difficult moment in a brand-new role is very different from evidence of fundamental incompetence. What would you say to a close friend or colleague who came to you with this exact same fear after their first major setback in a new job?

client: I mean, I'd probably tell a friend that one setback doesn't define them and that everyone struggles when they're new to something. But honestly, it feels different when it's me — like the rules don't apply the same way, and I know that sounds irrational but I can't just logic my way out of it. Hearing that it has a name, "impostor syndrome," is kind of interesting, but I'm not sure knowing what it's called actually changes how real it feels in my chest when I walk into the office.
therapist: You're showing real self-awareness by noticing that gap between what you'd tell a friend and how you treat yourself — and you're absolutely right that just naming something doesn't dissolve the feeling in your chest, because emotions aren't arguments you can win with logic alone. What CBT suggests is that we work *with* that feeling rather than trying to reason it away — noticing it, gently questioning the story it's telling, and slowly building small pieces of evidence that tell a different story over time. I'm wondering — when you think back over the past few weeks, even amid the chaos, is there one moment, however small, where you handled something in a way that a completely incompetent person simply couldn't have?

client: There was this moment last week where one of my team members was really panicking about a different deliverable, and I actually managed to calm them down and help them break the work into smaller pieces — they thanked me afterward. But my brain immediately jumps to "that's just basic stuff, anyone could have done that," and I kind of dismiss it before it even has a chance to mean anything. I guess I'm worried that building a case out of small moments like that is just going to feel like I'm convincing myself of something that isn't really true.
therapist: What you just did — talking someone through panic, breaking down complexity into clarity under pressure — is actually a core skill of effective leadership, and the fact that your brain labels it "basic" is the impostor syndrome doing its job of keeping the evidence from landing. Your worry about "convincing yourself of something untrue" is worth sitting with, but I'd gently flip it: you've already been convincing yourself of a story — that you don't belong — without demanding the same level of proof from *that* narrative. What if collecting these moments isn't about building a false case, but about finally giving the other side of the story a fair hearing?

client: That reframe actually hit me a little harder than I expected — the idea that I've been holding the "I don't belong" story to a completely different standard than any evidence against it. But I think the hard part is that collecting these small moments feels almost embarrassing, like I'd be keeping a little journal of "times I wasn't terrible," and I'm not sure I could take it seriously without cringing. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to do this that doesn't feel so... forced or artificial.
therapist: That instinct to cringe is really worth noticing — it's almost like a reflex to protect the impostor story by making the antidote feel silly before you even try it. What if instead of a formal "wins journal," you simply paused for ten seconds after a moment like the one with your teammate and just let it exist, without immediately filing it under "doesn't count"? I'm curious — what do you think that dismissal reflex is actually protecting you from, if you were to let those moments genuinely mean something?

client: I think if I let those moments actually mean something, I'd have to accept that maybe I do belong here — and then the stakes get even higher, because there's no excuse anymore if I fail again. It's almost safer to stay in the "I don't really deserve this" story because then a setback is expected, and I'm protected from the full weight of disappointment. That's kind of uncomfortable to say out loud, but I think that might be what's actually going on.
therapist: What you just uncovered is genuinely profound — the impostor story isn't just a fear, it's actually functioning as a shield, keeping the stakes feeling manageable by lowering your own expectations of yourself before anyone else can. That's a really honest and courageous thing to say out loud, and it makes complete sense as a strategy, even if it's costing you the ability to feel settled or capable in your own role. I'm wondering — if belonging here and being allowed to fail sometimes weren't mutually exclusive, if struggling didn't automatically mean you were right all along, what might it feel like to hold both of those things as true at once?

client: Honestly, sitting with that question feels really uncomfortable, like the ground isn't quite solid under me — because I think I've been using that shield for so long that I don't fully know who I am at work without it. The idea of belonging AND being allowed to fail sounds reasonable when you say it, but in practice I think my brain would still interpret every mistake as proof I was wrong to let my guard down. I want to believe those two things can coexist, but I'm not sure I trust myself to hold onto that when I'm actually in the middle of a hard moment at work.
therapist: That feeling of unsteady ground makes complete sense — you've just identified a belief system you've been living inside for a long time, and loosening it is disorienting even when it's the right thing to do. The trust you're describing isn't something that arrives all at once as a decision; it gets built in exactly those small moments, like the one with your teammate, where you act *as if* you belong and then notice that the ground held. I'm wondering — what would it look like to treat the next difficult moment at work not as a test of whether you truly belong, but as a small experiment in seeing whether you can survive a mistake without it meaning everything you fear it means?

client: I like the word "experiment" — it takes some of the weight off, because an experiment can fail and that's still useful data rather than a verdict. But I think my worry is that in the actual moment, when my heart is racing and I've just made a mistake in front of my team, I'm not going to remember to frame it as an experiment — I'm just going to feel the panic and go straight back to the old story. I guess I'm wondering if there's something more concrete I could practice now, before I'm in that situation, so it's not just an idea that disappears under pressure.
therapist: You're thinking about this in such a practical, grounded way — and you're right that insights formed in calm moments need to be rehearsed to be accessible when panic hits. One concrete thing you could try is crafting a single short phrase *now*, something like "this is data, not a verdict," that you practice saying to yourself regularly so it becomes almost automatic, a little anchor that's already familiar when the storm arrives. What words would feel most true and steadying to *you* — because the phrase will stick better if it's in your own language rather than mine?

client: I think the phrase that feels closest to true for me is something like "one moment doesn't write the whole story" — because that speaks to the specific fear I have about mistakes becoming permanent proof. But I'll be honest, I'm a little skeptical about whether repeating a phrase to myself is actually going to cut through the noise when I'm panicking in front of my team. I want to try it, but I guess I need to believe there's more to it than just words — like, does the repetition actually rewire something over time, or does it only work if I already half-believe it?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair, and I want to be honest with you — the phrase alone isn't magic, but what it actually does is create a tiny pause between the panic and the old story, and that pause is where your brain slowly learns that it has a choice rather than just a reflex. Over time, with repetition, that pause gets a little wider, and the new story gets a little more worn-in, not because you forced yourself to believe it but because you kept showing up and the catastrophe you feared didn't always arrive. I'm curious — you've already shown today that you can hold a new idea even when it feels uncomfortable and uncertain, so what would it mean to treat this phrase the same way, not as something you need to fully believe yet, but as something you're willing to keep testing?

client: I think framing it as something I'm "willing to keep testing" rather than something I have to believe right now actually makes it feel more manageable — like I'm not being asked to fake a confidence I don't have yet. I can probably commit to that, even if part of me is still waiting for the moment it doesn't work and I end up feeling like I was right to be skeptical all along. I guess what I'm taking away from today is that the skepticism itself doesn't have to be the enemy — it can just be another thing I'm noticing without letting it make all the decisions.
therapist: What you just articulated is genuinely a shift — you came in today feeling like you were drowning, and you're leaving with something more nuanced: that skepticism, fear, and even the impostor story can all be present without having to be in charge. That's not a small thing, and I want you to notice that you arrived at it yourself; I just asked the questions. As you head back into the week, I'm wondering — what's one moment, however ordinary, where you might practice letting "one moment doesn't write the whole story" exist alongside the skepticism, just to see what happens?
